transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Lina (Redwood SE), Alex (Cobalt ML Infra), Priya (Cobalt Eng Dir), Tom (Cobalt SRE), Ravi (Cobalt NLP)

Auto-generated summary: quick review of quantization tradeoffs, runtime perf numbers, concerns about accuracy regressions and KV cache behavior on on-prem VPC deployments. Next: benchmarks and pilot scheduling.

Topics: INT8 vs FP8, GPTQ/GPTQ-like approaches, AWQ, per-layer vs per-channel quantization, calibration datasets, latency vs throughput tradeoffs, KV cache warmup and eviction, batching strategies, H100/A100 kernel selection, private VPC/on-prem install constraints, encryption and KMS integration.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): hi everyone, thanks for joining; i'm maya, i'll run the intro. looking forward to walking through quantization approaches and runtime impact. ethan will drive the technical parts.
[00:15] Alex (Cobalt): hey thanks, quick context: we're running a 7b and a 13b family for summarization and routing; latency target 150ms p50 for 7b and 350ms p50 for 13b, with tight tail-latency needs. cost is also important — want to compare hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem.
[00:30] Ethan (Redwood): got it. quick agenda: review INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs, show our perf numbers on H100 and A100, discuss regression risk and calibration, then talk about VPC on-prem considerations and KV cache/batching. sound good?
[00:45] Priya (Cobalt): yes. also need to know how model fallbacks work if quantized variant underperforms in production.
[01:05] Ethan: good callout — we do policy-driven fallback. you can route by accuracy or latency; if a quantized model fails a quality gate we fall back to a FP16 or hosted replica. more on rollouts later.
[01:30] Lina (Redwood): quick note on naming — when i say GPTQ or g p t q, that's our reference to post-training quantization family (layer-wise, usually per-channel scales) and AWQ refers to the newer adaptive weight quantization approach we evaluated. sometimes speech got 'g p t q' in notes.
[02:00] Ravi (Cobalt): can you explain the basic accuracy delta we should expect for GPTQ vs AWQ for our workloads? we saw a 3-4% metric drop in a quick test.
[02:20] Ethan: sure — rough ballpark from our internal benchmarks: GPTQ (4-bit/INT4 style) often gives larger regressions on instruction-following tasks; GPTQ-INT8 variants are better. AWQ and newer 8-bit schemes aim to preserve accuracy with per-group scales and better outlier handling. for 8-bit AWQ vs FP16 we often see <1% BLEU/ROUGE-ish regression on common summarization prompts, whereas naive INT8 can be ~1-3% depending on layer sensitivity. numbers vary by model and prompt distribution.
[03:05] Tom (Cobalt): interesting — did you run these on our prompt shapes? our prompts tend to be long context and multiple prefix tokens which could affect KV cache sizes.
[03:20] Ethan: not yet on your exact prompt set. that's why action item for Alex to share 1k representative prompts. when we run on your set we'll report both generation quality and token-level log-prob deviations.
[03:45] Alex: ok we'll share that. also question: FP8 sounds promising — how stable are FP8 kernels across H100 vs A100?
[04:00] Ethan: FP8 support is more mature on H100 with tensor core support; on A100 it's less consistent. also FP8 reduces memory and can improve throughput, but you're trading quantization noise vs dynamic range. for some LLM layers FP8 gives near-lossless results, for others we see calibration drift. our runtime chooses kernels based on detected hardware and sequence length distribution (auto kernel selection).
[04:35] Priya: do you do per-layer tuning automatically? i.e., mix FP16/INT8 in a single model?
[04:50] Ethan: yes — Redwood's optimizer supports mixed-precision profiles. you can pin a profile we recommend (we call it 'conservative-8bit') that leaves sensitive layers in FP16/FP8 and quantizes the rest. we also have a 'throughput-8bit' more aggressive profile. both are tested against your eval set during a rollout.
[05:15] Lina: note — some of the sensitive layers are often the first and last attention blocks and feed-forward output layers. quantizing those naively increases hallucinations in instruction tasks.
[05:40] Ravi: what about GPTQ runtime complexity? i heard GPTQ can be slow for large models during conversion.
[05:55] Ethan: conversion time for GPTQ is heavier than straight 8-bit linear quant; it's usually an offline step — minutes to hours depending on model size and conversion hardware. AWQ's calibration can be quicker in many cases because of different algorithms, but still requires representative calibration data. important: conversion is offline; runtime doesn't pay that cost, only memory/perf gains apply at inference.
[06:30] Alex: can we stream responses with quantized models? our app uses streaming to show partial results.
[06:45] Maya: yes — Redwood supports streaming tokens from quantized models the same as FP16. latency of first token is influenced by KV cache warmup and batching.
[07:05] Tom: KV cache concerns — on on-prem VPC, what's the memory footprint for large batch sizes? our cluster has 80GB H100s but we want predictable tail-latency.
[07:25] Ethan: KV cache per request grows with sequence length; our runtime has continuous batching and prefix/KV caching to reuse cached KV for repeated prefixes. for long-context prompts you need to account for KV memory per concurrent request and a cache retention policy. we expose memory and retention knobs; for predictable tail-latency we recommend conservative batch sizes and smaller max-batch-latency.
[07:55] Priya: any numbers you can share? p50/p99 throughput on H100 for 13b with AWQ?
[08:10] Ethan: rough numbers from our lab: on H100, 13b AWQ with optimized kernels: p50 ~120ms for 1-token generation at batch=1 (single-stream), p99 ~380ms with concurrent load; throughput (tokens/sec) scales with batching — with batch of 8 we measured ~3.2k tokens/sec aggregated. caveat: those numbers assume warmed KV cache; cold starts are slower.
[08:50] Alex: warmed how long?
[08:55] Ethan: warmup depends on pattern; for repeated prefixes we see effective warm cache after a few similar requests. we can also pre-warm for known prompts.
[09:10] Ravi: calibration datasets: what size and content do you need for AWQ/GPTQ?
[09:25] Ethan: typically a few thousand tokens representative of your domain; for stable per-channel scales we like 1k-10k examples covering prompt prefixes and expected instruction patterns. we'll run quantization-aware evals using your prompts.
[09:50] Lina: also we'll compute delta metrics: per-prompt log-prob shift, rouge/accuracy deltas, and embedding cosine similarity when relevant.
[10:10] Priya: security: on-prem VPC with KMS — will quantized models expose any additional risk?
[10:25] Maya: quantization doesn't change data handling. our Private deployment runs a customer-managed control plane or an isolated control plane and supports KMS/HSM for model keys and S3 encryption. audit logs and RBAC are available. for on-prem we ship connector/helm charts and a package that runs in your cluster; HSM integration requires some ops work but is supported.
[10:55] Tom: does Redwood store any raw prompts during Dedicated/Private?
[11:05] Maya: in Private deployments, no logs leave your VPC unless you opt in. Dedicated has controls and can disable retention. we'll share SOC2 docs.
[11:20] Alex: about fallback policy again — what's the detection signal for a quality regression? do you compare against baseline generation or use an eval set in real-time?
[11:35] Ethan: you can configure multiple signals: 1) offline eval gating on a held-out prompt set with thresholds, 2) real-time business metrics, and 3) runtime heuristics like log-prob drops or unexpected token patterns. if threshold violated we can route to FP16 replicas or a hosted fallback.
[12:00] Ravi: any notes about AWQ vs GPTQ for instruction prompts specifically?
[12:10] Ethan: AWQ tends to handle outlier weights better and retains instruction-following behavior in many models; GPTQ can be more brittle unless you do per-layer knobs. empirically for summarization GPTQ-8bit tuned carefully and AWQ both can be within 1% of FP16, but mismatch depends on prompt length and model family.
[12:40] Priya: will Redwood provide conversion artifacts (like quantized checkpoints) for us to store in our registry?
[12:50] Lina: yes — we can output quantized model artifacts (named with profile/version) that you can store in your model registry. those artifacts include metadata about the profile and calibration data hash.
[13:10] Alex: about kernels — you mentioned runtime kernel selection. can you explain how sequence length influences kernel choice and latency?
[13:25] Ethan: sure — some kernels perform better for short sequences (less overhead) and others for long sequences where compute dominates. runtime picks the best kernel based on model size, hardware (A100/H100), and current sequence length distribution. this is automatic but tunable.
[13:50] Tom: do you support operator fusion for quantized ops?
[13:55] Ethan: yes, in our serving runtime we fuse matmul + quant-dequant paths where beneficial; fusion is gated by model architecture and kernel availability. yields lower overhead and better throughput.
[14:15] Ravi: what about tooling for regression detection? we'd like automated p0 alerts if rouge drops more than X.
[14:25] Maya: Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals on a perturbation set and create regression alerts tied to prompt sets/evals. we can integrate with your pager.
[14:40] Priya: rolling upgrades — if we convert a model to AWQ and serve it, how do we measure rollouts and revert?
[14:55] Ethan: we support canary rollouts with metrics-driven gates: you define early-warning metrics and an automatic rollback policy. you can also route a percentage of traffic to the quantized variant and increase on success.
[15:20] Alex: on operational cost — how much infra reduction should we expect moving 13b from FP16 to AWQ-8bit?
[15:35] Ethan: depends on batch shape and latency SLOs. rough rule: AWQ 8-bit can reduce memory footprint by ~40-45% compared to FP16 which can translate to 1.5-2x throughput improvement or fewer GPUs for same throughput. but tail-latency constraints sometimes require leaving some layers in FP16, so effective gains vary.
[16:05] Ravi: if we need deterministic reproducibility for audits, do quantized models produce deterministic outputs?
[16:20] Ethan: inference is deterministic given fixed RNG seeds and identical kernels; quantization introduces different numerics but deterministic if you fix the runtime config. small floating point differences can still change nondeterministic sampling, so seed controls are important.
[16:45] Priya: any pitfalls for on-prem GPU drivers / docker versions?
[16:55] Lina: yes — certain cuFFT/cuBLAS and driver combos can change kernel availability. we maintain a supported matrix (we'll share). for FP8/H100 you need specific NVIDIA driver and cuda versions; we'll coordinate versions during the pilot.
[17:20] Tom: bandwidth/data plane questions: is model fetching done over internal network? we want images pulled from local registry to avoid egress.
[17:35] Maya: for Private on-prem we recommend hosting quantized artifacts in your local registry; the control plane can be in customer VPC. there are options for full air-gapped installs.
[17:50] Alex: any success stories with customers using AWQ in Prod?
[17:55] Ethan: yes — a fintech customer moved their 13b routing model to AWQ and reduced GPU footprint by ~35% and kept downstream accuracy within thresholds; we can share anonymized numbers.
[18:15] Ravi: for our short timeline — we want to run a 2-week pilot. what would Redwood need from us?
[18:30] Maya: we need access to a representative prompt set, pilot cluster windows, and an SRE contact to coordinate install. we'll also need an NDAed channel for logs and traces.
[18:45] Alex: ok we'll get that to you.
[19:00] Ethan: one more technical note on batch sizing: continuous batching is good for throughput but harms tail-latency; we provide a batch shaping policy where you can set max-batch-latency, max-batch-size, and priority lanes for low-latency requests.
[19:25] Priya: about eviction — KV cache eviction policy when memory pressure hits?
[19:35] Ethan: LRU-ish with awareness of prefix popularity; we also support size-based eviction and TTL for entries. for mission-critical low-tail-latency paths we suggest pinning popular prefixes in a hot cache.
[19:55] Tom: any hooks for collecting perf traces? we want to compare to our internal profiler.
[20:05] Lina: yes — we can export per-request traces, token-level timing, and GPU kernel timelines. those are part of the pilot bundle.
[20:20] Alex: question — if GPTQ gives better compression but AWQ gives better quality, can we do hybrid artifacts in registry and route dynamically?
[20:35] Ethan: absolutely — you can keep multiple artifacts and route by policy or runtime A/B tests. we recommend a canary run to instrument QoE metrics before wide rollout.
[20:50] Ravi: how long will the conversion to AWQ take for our 13b?
[20:58] Ethan: typically a few hours on a beefy GPU node; we'll estimate precisely after we have your repo access and prompt sets.
[21:15] Priya: anything else on accuracy regressions — do you provide tooling to re-calibrate if regressions appear post-rollout?
[21:25] Ethan: yes — we run iterative re-calibration and per-layer overrides; the conversion artifacts include re-triggerable calibration scripts you can run in your environment.
[21:45] Alex: great. last — what would you recommend we start with?
[21:55] Lina: start with a conservative-8bit profile on the 7b family for summarization; run AWQ and GPTQ side-by-side on your prompt set, measure p50/p99 and quality deltas, then pick candidate for canary.
[22:15] Maya: to recap next steps: ethan will run AWQ vs GPTQ on provided 1k prompt set, maya will send pricing and SOC2/KMS docs, alex will provide prompts and pilot windows. we'll schedule the 2-hr pilot install during week of 11/30.
[22:40] Priya: thanks — this was helpful.
[22:45] Alex: thanks everyone.
[22:50] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with notes and the spreadsheet.
